docs.title: Splyne
docs.text:
Splyne is a local web application for guided RNA-seq analysis. It provides a Streamlit interface around curated preprocessing, nf-core and post-processing workflows, allowing users to configure, launch, monitor and retrieve bioinformatics analyses without interacting directly with the command line.

The application is designed for local execution on UNIX-like systems and for reproducible workflow execution through Nextflow-compatible dependency backends such as Apptainer, Docker or Conda.

docs.title: Workflow schema
docs.text: Splyne v.2 workflow overview

docs.title: Core Capabilities
docs.text:
• Guided upload and validation of FASTQ, BAM and CRAM inputs.
  • Automatic samplesheet generation for supported community-curated nf-core workflows.
  • Optional read preprocessing with fastp.
  • Integration with nf-core workflows for quality control, fusion detection, differential splicing and RNA variant calling.
  • Differential expression post-processing through a dedicated Nextflow and R/Quarto workflow.
  • Persistent recovery metadata for interrupted or orphaned runs.
  • Automatic result archiving with a simple download mechanism.

docs.title: Intended Users
docs.text:
Splyne is intended for researchers, students and bioinformatics users who need to execute RNA-seq workflows in a controlled local environment but prefer a graphical interface for routine configuration and result retrieval.

The application does not remove the computational requirements of the underlying pipelines. Users are still expected to run Splyne on a machine with sufficient CPU, memory and storage for RNA-seq workloads.

docs.title: Current Scope
docs.text:
Splyne focuses on short-read RNA-seq workflows using a fixed GRCh38/Gencode-46 reference setup. The current implementation is optimized for local files, local execution and controlled use on a workstation or laboratory server.

Note

This documentation describes the current application behavior. It is written as operational documentation for a production-like tool, while still acknowledging platform and workflow limitations.

docs.title: Do I upload individual files?
docs.text: No. Splyne expects users to select a directory. It scans the directory and detects supported read files automatically.

docs.title: Can I mix FASTQ and BAM/CRAM files?
docs.text: No. A dataset should contain only one input type class. Mixed raw and aligned reads are blocked to avoid ambiguous samplesheets.

docs.title: Can I use cloud paths?
docs.text: The application is designed for local files. Some nf-core workflows may support remote paths, but this is not the primary supported mode in Splyne.

docs.title: Where are my results?
docs.text: Completed workflow archives are available in Run History > Stored results.

docs.title: Where are references stored?
docs.text: Reference files are stored under temp_files/nf-core-temp/aws-references/.

docs.title: Can I change the genome build?
docs.text: The current implementation uses a fixed GRCh38/Gencode-46 setup to preserve reproducibility across workflows.

docs.title: What happens if I close the browser during a run?
docs.text: The process may continue running. Splyne writes a persistent run marker so that the Run Inspector can recover metadata about the previous run.

docs.title: Why are some actions disabled?
docs.text: Actions that could conflict with an active process are disabled while a long-running process is running.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide describes the standard execution path for a new analysis.

docs.title: 1. Start Splyne
docs.text:
Open a terminal, activate the environment and launch Splyne from the app directory:

# Activate the dedicated Conda environment
conda activate splyne-v2-env

# Launch Splyne by calling streamlit run
streamlit run splyne_app.py

Splyne will run locally and automatically open in your default web browser. If the application does not pop up automatically, navigate to the URL displayed by Streamlit in the terminal.

docs.title: 2. Upload Input Data
docs.text:
Go to Input > Upload files and select the directory containing the sequencing files.

Supported input formats:

  • .fastq
  • .fq
  • .fastq.gz
  • .fq.gz
  • .bam
  • .cram

All input files should be located in the same directory. Splyne will detect files automatically (if any) and generate a samplesheet that can be reviewed and edited before execution.

docs.title: 3. Review the Samplesheet
docs.text:
After detection, Splyne displays an editable table. Review each row carefully:

  • Confirm that sample names are correct.
  • Confirm that paired-end files are matched correctly.
  • Set strandedness and condition fields where relevant.
  • Save the samplesheet before continuing.

docs.title: 4. Fetch References
docs.text:
Go to Preprocessing > Genomic references if the selected workflows require reference files.

Splyne will check for the availability of the required reference files. If they are missing, use the corresponding page action to retrieve them. If this is not the first time running the application and the references have already been successfully downloaded, they will be automatically detected and selected.

docs.title: 5. Optional Read Preprocessing
docs.text:
Go to Preprocessing > Read filtering to run fastp on raw paired-end FASTQ files.

If read filtering is completed, downstream workflows can use the cleaned samplesheet generated from the filtered FASTQ files.

docs.title: 6. Run an Analysis Workflow
docs.text:
Choose one of the analysis modules:

  • quality control
  • gene fusions
  • differential splicing
  • variant calling
  • differential expression

Each module exposes default settings and an advanced configuration section. Default parameters are intended to provide a safe baseline for routine execution, although users are encouraged to review the advanced configuration section to select the options most appropriate for their analytical goals.

docs.title: 7. Monitor Execution
docs.text:
When a workflow is running, Splyne marks the process as active in the sidebar. The active process can be monitored from the workflow page through the Nextflow log popover.

Info

Only one long-running process is managed at a time. Consult Architecture > Job Manager for more info.

If the app is closed during a run, use Run History > Run inspector to inspect, archive, terminate or close the recovered run marker.

docs.title: 8. Retrieve Results
docs.text: When a workflow finishes, Splyne packages selected outputs into a ZIP archive. Go to Run History > Stored results to download or remove completed run archives.

docs.title: Annotation
docs.text: Structured biological information associated with genomic coordinates, such as genes, transcripts, exons or variant consequences.

docs.title: Apptainer
docs.text: Container runtime commonly used in scientific and HPC environments. Splyne uses Apptainer as the default Nextflow execution profile because it provides reproducible software environments without requiring a daemon.

docs.title: BAM
docs.text: Binary Alignment Map. A compressed binary format for aligned sequencing reads.

docs.title: Base Recalibration
docs.text: Variant-calling preprocessing step that adjusts sequencing quality scores using known variation resources. In Splyne, this is relevant to RNA variant calling when the required variation files are available.

docs.title: Conda
docs.text: Package and environment manager used to install Splyne's Python and command-line dependencies. Conda can also be selected as a Nextflow profile, although container-based profiles are generally preferred for nf-core workflows.

docs.title: CRAM
docs.text: Reference-based compressed format for aligned sequencing reads. CRAM files normally require access to the corresponding reference genome for interpretation.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text: Container runtime supported by Nextflow and nf-core. Docker is suitable for local machines where the Docker engine is available and properly configured.

docs.title: FASTQ
docs.text: Text format containing sequencing reads and per-base quality scores. FASTQ is the standard input format for raw short-read sequencing data.

docs.title: fastp
docs.text: Read preprocessing tool used by Splyne for quality filtering, trimming and report generation from paired-end FASTQ files.

docs.title: GATK
docs.text: Genome Analysis Toolkit. A widely used toolkit for variant calling and filtering workflows.

docs.title: Gencode
docs.text: Reference genome annotation project used by several RNA-seq workflows integrated in Splyne.

docs.title: GRCh38
docs.text: Human genome reference assembly used by the current Splyne reference setup.

docs.title: Long-Running Process
docs.text: A process that may take minutes or hours to complete, such as a Nextflow workflow, reference download or read preprocessing task.

docs.title: MultiQC
docs.text: Tool that aggregates quality-control reports from multiple bioinformatics tools into a single summary report.

docs.title: Nextflow
docs.text: Workflow management system used by nf-core pipelines. Splyne builds Nextflow commands and delegates workflow execution to Nextflow.

docs.title: nf-core
docs.text: Community collection of curated, reproducible Nextflow pipelines following shared standards for configuration, documentation and outputs.

docs.title: Process ID
docs.text: Operating system identifier assigned to a running process. Splyne stores process IDs to monitor and recover active runs.

docs.title: Run Archive
docs.text: ZIP file generated by Splyne after workflow completion. It contains selected output files according to workflow-specific filtering rules.

docs.title: Run Registry
docs.text: Persistent JSON marker used by Splyne to recover active run metadata after a browser refresh, app restart or interrupted session.

docs.title: Samplesheet
docs.text: CSV file describing samples, input files and metadata required by nf-core pipelines.

docs.title: snpEff
docs.text: Variant annotation tool that predicts and annotates variant effects using reference databases.

docs.title: STAR
docs.text: Spliced Transcripts Alignment to a Reference. A high-performance RNA-seq aligner used by several workflows.

docs.title: Streamlit
docs.text: Python framework used to build Splyne's local web interface.

docs.title: VCF
docs.text: Variant Call Format. Standard text format for storing genomic variants.

docs.title: VEP
docs.text: Variant Effect Predictor. Annotation tool used to predict functional consequences of genomic variants.

docs.title: Workflow Profile
docs.text: Execution backend selected for a Nextflow run, such as apptainer, docker or conda.

docs.title: Job Manager
docs.text: The job manager is the runtime component responsible for launching, monitoring and finalizing long-running processes.

docs.title: Session State Contract
docs.text:
The active job is stored in st.session_state.job_state. Its fields include:

  • state: idle, running, done or archiving.
  • pipeline: active workflow name.
  • pid: operating system process identifier.
  • process: subprocess.Popen object.
  • returncode: process exit code.
  • workdir: workflow work directory.
  • resultsdir: workflow output directory.
  • ft_path: path to output filtering patterns.
  • zip_launched: archiving flag.
  • runid: generated run identifier.

The UI uses this state to disable unsafe actions while a process is running.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> idle
    idle --> running: launch workflow
    running --> done: process exits
    done --> archiving: launch result archiver
    archiving --> idle: archive completed
    running --> done: user cancellation

docs.title: Process Control
docs.text:
Splyne launches workflow processes in a new process session. This makes it possible to stop a process group when the user cancels an active workflow.

The sidebar displays the current process status and exposes a stop action when a long-running process is active.

docs.title: Archiving
docs.text:
After a workflow exits, Splyne creates a ZIP archive containing selected outputs. Archive names follow the structure {run_id}_{pipeline}_{exit-status}.zip where:

  • run_id - generated run ID
  • pipeline - pipeline name
  • exit-status - execution status

Example: 

run_27052026_203444_nf-core-rnavar_success.zip

See Results for more details.

docs.title: Operational Limitation
docs.text: The current manager is intentionally single-job. It is designed to prevent simultaneous pipeline launches from the same UI session. The fundamental reason behind this design is the heavy computational burden of nf-core workflows. Permitting multiple concurrent executions in a local application could easily exhaust system resources, reduce overall stability, and negatively impact execution performance. Moreover, this approach reduces ambiguity in logs, simplifies state management, and improves result archiving and traceability.

docs.title: System Overview
docs.text:
Splyne is organized as a Streamlit multi-page application with a small orchestration layer for external tools and workflow execution.

At runtime, the application coordinates four main responsibilities:

  • Input discovery and samplesheet generation.
  • User interaction and workflow configuration.
  • Launching and monitoring external processes.
  • Packaging and preserving workflow results.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    User["User browser"] --> UI["Streamlit UI"]
    UI --> State["Session state"]
    UI --> Inputs["Input detection and samplesheets"]
    UI --> Jobs["Job manager"]
    Jobs --> Processes["External processes"]
    Processes --> NF["Nextflow / fastp / shell tools"]
    Jobs --> Registry["Persistent run registry"]
    Processes --> Results["Workflow outputs"]
    Results --> Archiver["Result archiver"]
    Archiver --> History["Stored result ZIP files"]

docs.title: Interface Layer
docs.text: The interface is defined by Streamlit pages registered in splyne_app.py. Each page represents a functional module such as file upload, preprocessing, workflow execution or result management.

docs.title: Workflow Layer
docs.text: Procedural pages generate command-line calls for Nextflow, fastp, or auxiliary scripts. To simplify the management of Nextflow processes, a Workflow object is used to encapsulate the command and execution-related parameters. In contrast, simpler processes, such as fastp, pigz, or other command-line utilities, as well as genomic reference retrieval tasks, are directly managed within their respective pages.

docs.title: Execution Layer
docs.text: Long-running commands are launched using subprocess.Popen and monitored across Streamlit reruns through a dedicated job manager. The active process state is stored in st.session_state, ensuring persistence and idempotency across script executions.

docs.title: Recovery Layer
docs.text: The run registry persists active run metadata to disk. This allows Splyne to detect a previous run after an app restart or browser reload.

docs.title: Result Layer
docs.text: Completed outputs are filtered and archived into ZIP files under temp_files/stored_results. The Run History page provides access to these archives.

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
• Keep the command-line workflow engine visible but not exposed to routine users.
  • Use reproducible workflow definitions and reference datasets with fixed versions.
  • Prefer local files and local execution for simplicity, privacy and predictability.
  • Avoid running multiple long-running workflows concurrently from the same UI session.

docs.title: Run Registry
docs.text: The run registry is a persistent JSON marker used to recover information about an active or recently interrupted run.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Streamlit session state is volatile. If the browser is reloaded, the app is restarted or a previous process is still running, session state alone is insufficient.

The registry solves this by storing minimal run metadata on disk.

docs.title: Registry Location
docs.text:
The active run marker is stored at:

temp_files/run_registry.json

docs.title: Stored Metadata
docs.text:
The registry contains:

  • run_id
  • pipeline
  • pid
  • workdir
  • resultsdir
  • ft_path
  • nf_log
  • state
  • returncode
  • started_at
  • updated_at

docs.title: Status Inference
docs.text:
When the Run Inspector opens, Splyne checks whether the recorded process ID is still alive.

Possible inferred statuses:

  • running
  • success*
  • cancelled*
  • finished-or-unknown
  • missing

*Inference of the final process exit state is not always possible. Since pipeline executions are launched as detached background processes, Splyne loses direct access to the original process handle if the UI session ends or the application is restarted. In such cases, although the process can still be detected through its PID, the operating system returncode cannot always be reliably recovered. As a consequence, completed executions may sometimes be classified as finished-or-unknown instead of a definitive success or cancelled state.

docs.title: Recovery Actions
docs.text:
The Run Inspector can:

  • refresh status
  • archive available results
  • terminate a running process
  • erase intermediate files
  • close the run marker

Warning

The registry is a recovery aid, not a full provenance database. It stores operational metadata required to reconnect the UI with a previous process.

docs.title: State Management
docs.text:
Splyne combines two complementary state mechanisms:

  • Streamlit session state for interactive, per-browser-session continuity.
  • A disk-backed run registry for recovering long-running processes after the UI is refreshed or restarted.

Most UI state lives in st.session_state. This object behaves like a mutable dictionary that persists across Streamlit reruns for the same user session. Since Streamlit re-executes the active script after most interactions, Splyne uses session state as the contract between pages: the input page records which files are ready, workflow pages check those flags before enabling analysis, and the sidebar reads the active process state to disable unsafe actions while a command is running.

Session state is intentionally treated as runtime state, not as permanent storage. Values can be cleared by the app reset action, by selecting a new input directory, or by restarting the browser session. Anything that must survive beyond the Streamlit session is stored on disk, either as files under temp_files/ or as active-run metadata in the run registry.

docs.title: State Categories
docs.text:
Splyne uses session state for four main concerns:

  • Input progression: selected directory, detected reads, compression status, ready files and samplesheet status.
  • Execution control: the single active long-running process stored in job_state.
  • Workflow UI memory: working directory selections, preprocessing flags and toast suppression flags.
  • Widget state: explicit Streamlit widget keys such as data editors and per-run action buttons.

The tables below list the explicit session-state keys used by Splyne. Streamlit may also create internal widget identifiers for widgets that do not define a custom key; those implementation-generated keys are not part of the application contract.

docs.title: Application Shell
docs.text:
These keys are initialized by splyne_app.py and are available from the main application frame.

Key Initial value Type Purpose job_state job-manager default dictionary dict Single active process state shared across pages and the sidebar. screen_mode sidebar str Navigation layout selected by the user: sidebar, top or hidden. previous_run_toast_shown False bool Prevents repeated previous-run recovery notifications during reruns.

The app reset button calls st.session_state.clear(), removes selected temporary analysis files, and reruns the app. Reset controls are disabled while job_state["state"] is not idle.

docs.title: Input State
docs.text:
The input page (file_loading.py) owns the state that gates all downstream workflows. It initializes the keys below through a default banner dictionary and updates them as the user selects a directory, files are detected, FASTQ files are compressed, and the samplesheet is generated.

Key Initial value Type Updated by Purpose dir_path None str \| None Directory selector Absolute or user-selected path containing input read files. read_files None list[str] \| None Read detection File names detected in dir_path with supported read extensions. reads_scanned False bool Read detection Marks that the selected directory has already been scanned. fastq_gz_done False bool Compression step Marks that FASTQ inputs are already gzip-compressed or did not need compression. gz_paths None list[str] \| None Input defaults Reserved top-level placeholder for compressed FASTQ paths. The active compression process also stores gz_paths inside job_state. all_reads None tuple[str, ...] \| None Compression step Complete set of available read paths used as selectable values in samplesheet editors. ready_files None tuple[str, ...] \| list[str] \| None Compression and samplesheet editing Current input files accepted for downstream workflows. Can be narrowed after samplesheet edits. file_type None str \| None Samplesheet creation Detected input family used to decide samplesheet columns and validation rules. samplesheet_ready False bool Samplesheet creation Signals that temp_files/samplesheet.csv exists and downstream pages can proceed.

Downstream pages use the pair below as their main guard:

upload_correct = (
    st.session_state.get("ready_files", False)
    and st.session_state.get("samplesheet_ready", False)
)

If this guard fails, the page stops before exposing workflow controls. This prevents workflows from launching without a validated input set.

docs.title: Preprocessing State
docs.text:
read_trimming.py adds flags that describe the optional FASTQ preprocessing stage.

Key Initial value Type Purpose ss_fastp False bool Tracks whether the clean samplesheet has been produced after fastp trimming. current_fastp None str \| None Tracks the current sample name to make it persistent to st.rerun(). clean_paths None tuple \| None Tracks the definitive paths to fastp-filtered reads to make them persistent to st.rerun().

docs.title: Workflow State
docs.text:
Workflow pages share a small set of session-state keys for working directory selection and one-time notifications.

Module Key Initial value Type Purpose nf-core-demo.py wd_path None str \| None Selected Nextflow working directory for QC/demo execution. rnafusion.py wd_path None str \| None Selected Nextflow working directory for RNA fusion execution. rnasplice.py wd_path None str \| None Selected Nextflow working directory for RNA splicing execution. rnasplice.py bt_toast False bool Suppresses repeated BAM/BAI-related warning toasts. rnavar.py wd_path None str \| None Selected Nextflow working directory for RNA variant calling execution. rnavar.py br_toast False bool Suppresses repeated BAM-readiness warning toasts. rnavar.py annot_toast False bool Suppresses repeated annotation-cache warning toasts.

wd_path is reused by several workflow pages under the same key name. This means the last selected working directory can be carried between those pages during the same Streamlit session.

docs.title: Job State
docs.text:
The active process manager is stored as a nested dictionary in st.session_state.job_state. It is initialized by py_scripts/job_manager.py and read or updated by workflow pages, the input compression step and the sidebar.

Field Initial value Type Purpose state idle str Process lifecycle state: idle, running, done or archiving. pipeline None str \| None Name of the active workflow or utility process. pid None int \| None Operating-system process identifier. process None subprocess.Popen \| None Live subprocess object monitored across reruns. returncode None int \| None Process exit code once available. workdir None Path \| None Nextflow work directory used by the active workflow. resultsdir None Path \| None Directory containing workflow outputs. ft_path None Path \| None File containing output extensions used by the result archiver. zip_launched False bool Archive-launch guard for completed workflow processes. runid None str \| None Generated run identifier used by the run registry and ZIP filename. gz_paths not present by default list[str] Temporary field used only by the pigz_compression input utility process.

job_state is deliberately single-job. When state is not idle, launch buttons and reset actions are disabled or redirected so that only one long-running process is controlled by the session at a time. See Job Manager for the full lifecycle and archiving behavior.

docs.title: Widget State
docs.text:
Some Streamlit widgets use explicit keys. These keys are managed by Streamlit and may appear in st.session_state, but they should be treated as UI widget state rather than business logic.

Module Key or pattern Widget Purpose Workflow pages wd_selector st.form Form state for selecting the workflow work directory. dea_postprocessing.py gc_editor st.data_editor Display state for the gene-counts table preview. dea_postprocessing.py metadata_editor st.data_editor Editable metadata table state. run_history.py download_<run_id> st.download_button Per-run stored-results download button state. run_history.py erase_<run_id> st.button Per-run stored-results deletion button state.

docs.title: Persistent State
docs.text:
Session state is not sufficient for process recovery because it disappears when the Streamlit session is lost. For long-running workflows, Splyne writes active-run metadata under temp_files/app_state/ through the run registry. The registry stores the run ID, process ID, pipeline name, work directory, results directory and log paths needed by the recovery inspector.

This disk state is only used when interactive session state cannot be trusted, such as after an application restart. Normal workflow execution still uses st.session_state.job_state as the primary runtime source of truth.

docs.title: Reset Behavior
docs.text:
Splyne has two reset patterns:

  • Input reset: selecting a new input directory refreshes the input defaults and replaces dir_path.
  • Application reset: the sidebar reset action clears all session-state keys, removes selected temporary files and reruns the app.

Caution

Resetting the application should not be used while a workflow is running. The UI disables reset controls when a long-running process is active.

docs.title: Workflow Engine
docs.text:
Splyne does not reimplement workflow execution. It delegates heavy bioinformatics processing to external tools:

  • Nextflow for nf-core and post-processing workflows.
  • fastp for read preprocessing.
  • Shell scripts for reference retrieval and auxiliary system tasks.

docs.title: Workflow Declaration
docs.text:
Nextflow workflows are described in the application through a Workflow data structure containing:

  • name: internal workflow identifier.
  • command: command-line argument list.
  • workdir: Nextflow work directory.
  • resultsdir: output directory.
  • filetypes: output file patterns selected for archiving.
  • nf_log: Nextflow log path.
  • env: optional environment variables.

This structure allows workflow pages to define commands while delegating execution and monitoring to a shared manager.

docs.title: Execution Model
docs.text:
When a user launches a workflow:

  1. The workflow page builds the command.
  2. The job manager creates the required directories.
  3. Output filtering patterns are written to filetypes.txt.
  4. The command is launched as a background process.
  5. A persistent run marker is written to the run registry.
  6. Streamlit reruns periodically and checks process status.
  7. On completion, the archiver packages selected results.

docs.title: Nextflow Profiles
docs.text:
Most nf-core workflows support a dependency profile:

  • apptainer
  • docker
  • conda

Apptainer is the default profile in Splyne. Users may select another profile when available, but compatibility depends on the installed tools and the selected pipeline.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text: Nextflow logs are read from .nextflow.log by default and displayed from the workflow page. Splyne shows the latest log lines while the process is running and the full log when archiving begins.

docs.title: Genomic References
docs.text: All genomic references required by Splyne workflows are centralized in a single directory structure. This approach avoids data duplication, simplifies maintenance, and reduces storage requirements by allowing multiple workflows to share common resources.

docs.title: Amazon Web Services
docs.text:
The core reference bundle is derived from the reference set distributed with the nf-core/rnafusion workflow, which provides all resources required to run the pipeline and is publicly available through Amazon Web Services (AWS). The bundle was later extended with variant annotation caches and known-variation databases required by nf-core/rnavar. Together, these resources form the complete reference set used by Splyne, whose organization is illustrated bellow.

nf-core-temp/
└── aws-references
    └── GRCh38
        ├── arriba
        │   └── 2.5.0
        ├── fusion_report_db
        │   ├── cosmic.db
        │   ├── DB-timestamp.txt
        │   ├── fusiongdb2.db
        │   ├── fusion_report.log
        │   └── mitelman.db
        ├── gencode_v46
        │   ├── fusioncatcher
        │   ├── gencode
        │   ├── gffread
        │   ├── salmon
        │   ├── star
        │   └── starfusion
        └── hgnc
            ├── hgnc_complete_set.txt
            └── HGNC-DB-timestamp.txt

nf-core-rnavar-temp/
├── annot-cache
│   ├── snpeff_cache
│   │   └── GRCh38.99
│   └── vep_cache
│       └── homo_sapiens
└── variation
    ├── dbsnp_146.hg38.vcf.gz
    ├── dbsnp_146.hg38.vcf.gz.tbi
    ├── Mills_and_1000G_gold_standard.indels.hg38.vcf.gz
    └── Mills_and_1000G_gold_standard.indels.hg38.vcf.gz.tbi

Warning

The required reference datasets are substantial in size and may become a limiting factor on systems with insufficient available storage. The references needed for the nf-core/rnafusion workflow alone occupy approximately 150 GB of free disk space, with an additional 4 GB required for nf-core/rnavar–specific reference files.

docs.title: Reference retrieval
docs.text:
The logic for reference retrieval is encapsulated within the Preprocessing > Genomic References section of the application.

Splyne automatically detects whether the required references have already been downloaded. If no references are found, a simple interface is displayed that allows users to initiate the download process. Once started, reference retrieval is managed autonomously as a standalone background task. The Conda environment designed for Splyne includes the AWS CLI package, which is used to download and synchronize the required reference datasets directly from the AWS-hosted repositories.

Reference retrieval is performed using the following command:

aws --no-sign-request s3 sync <SOURCE> <LOCAL_DESTINATION>

Users only need to ensure that the references are available locally before launching a workflow. Once downloaded, the same reference set can be reused across all analyses supported by the application.

docs.title: Supported Platforms
docs.text:
Splyne is designed for Linux-based or UNIX-compatible environments. The interface is built with Streamlit, but the execution layer depends on tools and conventions that are most reliable on Linux systems.

Recommended platforms:

  • Ubuntu or another Linux distribution with Conda/Mamba support.
  • Linux workstation or server with access to local storage.
  • UNIX-compatible development systems for testing, with the understanding that full workflow compatibility depends on container and Nextflow support.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Main dependencies:

  • Python 3.12
  • Streamlit
  • Nextflow
  • fastp
  • pigz
  • awscli
  • psutil
  • pysam
  • pandas
  • st-annotated-text

Although manual installation of dependencies is possible, a dedicated Conda environment, splyne-v2-env, is provided for Splyne to be reproducible and to simplify its setup. It includes all necessary dependencies required for running the webtool and it is designed to be as lightweight as possible to ensure correct and consistent resolution of the dependency graph across different computational environments.

A pre-defined environment specification file is included with the Splyne installation, at versions/environment.yml.

docs.title: Hardware Recommendations
docs.text:
Minimum practical configuration:

  • 16 CPU cores
  • 64 GB RAM
  • 1 TB SSD storage

Recommended configuration for larger RNA-seq workloads:

  • 24-32 CPU cores
  • 128 GB RAM
  • 2 TB or more of fast SSD/NVMe storage

RNA-seq pipelines, specially Nextflow ones, can generate large temporary directories. Ensure that the filesystem containing temp_files/ has sufficient free space before running analyses.

docs.title: Install from Source
docs.text:
Clone the repository:

git clone https://github.com/pablolopeznie/splyne.git
cd splyne

Create and activate the environment:

conda env create -f versions/environment.yml
conda activate splyne-v2-env

Start the application:

streamlit run splyne_app.py

Streamlit will print the local URL where the application is available.

docs.title: Dependency Backend
docs.text:
The underlying nf-core software stack is managed by Nextflow through the use of execution profiles. Splyne exposes these dependency profiles directly to enable seamless configuration of workflow execution environments. This allows users to select the most appropriate backend depending on their computational infrastructure.

Apptainer (formerly Singularity) is the default execution backend. It is widely used in bioinformatics environments due to its portability, interoperability, security model, and ability to run containerized workflows without requiring a continuously running daemon.

Supported profiles:

  • apptainer
  • docker
  • conda

Warning

Conda-only execution is not guaranteed to be supported by every nf-core workflow. For the maximum reproducibility, use Apptainer or Docker whenever possible.

docs.title: Reference Data
docs.text:
Several workflows require reference files before they can run. Reference retrieval is handled from the Genomic References page inside Splyne.

The current reference setup is fixed to GRCh38/Gencode-46 resources to preserve consistency across runs. See more in the dedicated section: Genomic References.

docs.title: Starting the App
docs.text:
conda activate splyne-v2-env
streamlit run splyne_app.py

docs.title: Normal Shutdown
docs.text: Use the sidebar shutdown control when possible. This allows Splyne to terminate managed processes and clear selected temporary files.

docs.title: Active Processes
docs.text:
When a long-running process is active:

  • the sidebar displays an active status badge
  • conflicting UI actions are disabled
  • the active process can be stopped from the sidebar
  • nextflow log becomes available in the page of the launched workflow

docs.title: Temporary Files
docs.text:
Splyne uses temp_files/ for:

  • generated samplesheets
  • internal communication files
  • intermediate workflow directories
  • reference resources
  • result archives
  • active run registry

This directory is part of the application runtime state.

docs.title: Reference Management
docs.text:
Reference files are expected under:

temp_files/nf-core-temp/aws-references/

The .complete.txt marker is used together with the expected reference directory to determine whether references are ready.

docs.title: Recovery Workflow
docs.text:
If Splyne detects a previous active run:

  1. Open Run History > Run inspector.
  2. Review pipeline, PID and paths.
  3. Refresh status if needed.
  4. Kill the process only if it is still running and should be terminated.
  5. Archive results if the process completed.
  6. Close the marker after recovery is complete.

docs.title: Streamlit Command Not Found
docs.text:
Ensure the Conda environment is active:

conda activate splyne-v2-env
streamlit run splyne_app.py

docs.title: No Files Detected
docs.text:
Check that:

  • files are in the selected directory
  • file extensions are supported
  • files are not hidden
  • files are not inside nested subdirectories

docs.title: Samples Are Parsed Incorrectly
docs.text:
Review file names. Avoid underscores inside sample names and use _R1 / _R2 for paired-end FASTQ files.

Warning

Sticking to Splyne file naming conventions is crutial for automatic detection. See more at Worflows > Input.

docs.title: Mixed File Type Error
docs.text: Splyne expects one input class per dataset. Do not mix raw FASTQ files with BAM or CRAM files in the same selected directory.

docs.title: References Not Found
docs.text:
Open Preprocessing > Genomic references and check whether reference retrieval has completed.

If retrieval failed, verify:

  • internet access
  • available disk space
  • app permissions on temp_files/

docs.title: Workflow Fails Immediately
docs.text:
Check:

  • selected dependency profile
  • Apptainer or Docker availability
  • samplesheet content
  • reference path readiness
  • .nextflow.log

docs.title: Run Still Appears After Restart
docs.text: Open Run History > Run inspector. The app may have detected a persistent run marker. Use the inspector to refresh, archive, close or terminate the run.

docs.title: Disk Space Issues
docs.text:
RNA-seq workflows may generate large intermediate files. Free disk space by:

  • deleting old archives from Run History
  • clearing intermediate directories after confirming results are archived
  • using a larger Nextflow work directory through advanced options

docs.title: Github API Rate Limit Exceeded
docs.text:
When interacting with nf-core pipelines through automated tools (e.g., pipeline downloaders, version checkers, or metadata resolvers), you may encounter the error:

GitHub API Rate Limit Exceeded

This error occurs because nf-core pipelines are distributed and versioned via GitHub, and the GitHub API enforces a limit on the number of requests that can be made within a given time window without authenticated access.

This issue is more likely to occur when:

  • Running multiple nf-core commands in a short time window
  • Running automated workflows that repeatedly query pipeline metadata

How to mitigate it: Wait for the rate limit to reset. GitHub rate limits are temporary and typically reset automatically after a short period (usually within an hour).

Info

There is a definite solution to this issue, although it may not be straightforward for users with limited computational experience. The most effective way to avoid this limitation is to use a GitHub personal access token, which increases the allowed number of API requests.

To apply this fix, you need to generate a token from a dedicated GitHub account and export it as an environment variable:

export GITHUB_TOKEN=your_token_here

Once set, nf-core tools will automatically use this token for authenticated requests, significantly reducing the likelihood of hitting rate limits.

docs.title: Filtering Logic
docs.text:
Splyne does not archive entire workflow output directories by default. Instead, each executable workflow declares a small set of result patterns that define which files are relevant enough to be preserved in the final ZIP archive.

This design keeps downloads manageable, avoids storing large intermediate files by accident and focuses the Run History module on reports, tables and interpretable outputs.

docs.title: Filtering Workflow
docs.text: The result filtering process is applied after a managed workflow finishes.

docs.title: Where Patterns Are Stored
docs.text:
Each workflow page defines an allowed_ft collection. When the workflow is launched, the job manager writes these patterns to:

<workflow_temp_directory>/filetypes.txt

For example, for an rnavar run the file is written next to the workflow run/results directories under:

temp_files/nf-core-rnavar-temp/filetypes.txt

The run registry stores the path to this file as ft_path, allowing the Run Inspector to reuse the same filtering rules during recovery.

docs.title: How Matching Works
docs.text:
The archiver reads filetypes.txt, splits the comma-separated patterns and scans the workflow output directory recursively.

Internally, each file path is tested with Python's Path.match():

found_match = any(file_path.match(pattern) for pattern in filetypes)

If a file matches at least one pattern, it is added to the ZIP archive while preserving its path relative to the workflow output directory.

Note

Patterns are filename/path glob patterns, not regular expressions. Examples include *.html, *.csv, *.vcf.gz and params*.json.

docs.title: nf-core/demo
docs.text:
The quality-control demo workflow keeps only HTML reports by default.

Pattern What it captures Why it is kept *.html HTML reports Main human-readable QC output.

docs.title: nf-core/rnafusion
docs.text:
Default rnafusion archive patterns:

Pattern What it captures Why it is kept *.html HTML reports Human-readable reports and summaries. *.tsv Tab-separated result tables Structured fusion and summary outputs. *.pdf PDF reports or plots Static visual outputs. *.txt Text summaries and logs published as results Lightweight metadata and tool summaries. *.sf Salmon quantification files Quantification outputs used by downstream fusion interpretation. *.vcf Variant/fusion call representations in VCF format Structured event records when generated. params*.json Pipeline parameter snapshots Reproducibility metadata.

Additional patterns added when Store alignments in binary format BAM is enabled:

Pattern What it captures Consequence *.Aligned.sortedByCoord.out.bam STAR coordinate-sorted BAM files Adds large alignment files to the archive. *.Aligned.sortedByCoord.out.bam.bai BAM indexes Required for efficient BAM inspection. *.Chimeric.out.junction STAR chimeric junction files Useful for inspecting fusion-supporting alignments. *.SJ.out.tab STAR splice junction tables Adds splice junction evidence.

rnafusion also requests additional recovery of files from a work-directory folder named:

microH_expr_brkpt_plots

The directory contains personalized graphics and plots from fusioninspector tool, intentionally produced to evaluate the consistency of the fusions detected by inspecting the fusion breakpoints. These files are copied into extra_splyne/ inside the output directory before the ZIP is created.

docs.title: nf-core/rnasplice
docs.text:
Default rnasplice archive patterns:

Pattern What it captures Why it is kept *.html HTML reports Main report output. *.txt* Text files, including compressed or suffixed text outputs Tool summaries and text-based results. *.pdf PDF plots or reports Static visual outputs. *.tsv Tab-separated tables Structured result tables. *.csv CSV tables Structured result tables. *.sf Salmon quantification files Quantification outputs. rmats*.log rMATS logs Diagnostic information for splicing analysis. *.dpsi Delta PSI outputs Splicing effect-size results. *.psivec PSI vector outputs Splicing inclusion summaries. *.psi PSI outputs Percent-spliced-in values. *.tpm TPM expression files Expression summaries. *.ioe SUPPA event annotation files Event-level splicing annotation. params*.json Pipeline parameter snapshots Reproducibility metadata.

Additional patterns added when Store alignments in binary format BAM is enabled:

Pattern What it captures Consequence *.sorted.bam Sorted BAM files Adds large alignment files to the archive. *.sorted.bam.bai BAM indexes Required for efficient BAM inspection.

Additional patterns added when Save R objects is enabled:

Pattern What it captures Consequence *.rds Serialized R objects Useful for downstream R analysis, but may increase archive size.

docs.title: nf-core/rnavar
docs.text:
Default rnavar archive patterns:

Pattern What it captures Why it is kept *.html HTML reports Human-readable workflow reports. *.vcf.gz Compressed VCF files Main variant call outputs. *.vcf.gz.tbi Tabix indexes for compressed VCF files Required for indexed VCF browsing. *.ann.tab.gz Compressed annotation tables Variant annotation outputs. *.txt Text summaries Lightweight summaries and metadata. *.csv CSV tables Structured result tables. params*.json Pipeline parameter snapshots Reproducibility metadata.

Additional patterns added when Store alignments in binary format BAM is enabled:

Pattern What it captures Consequence *.aligned.bam Aligned BAM files Adds large alignment files to the archive. *.aligned.bam.bai BAM indexes Required for efficient BAM inspection.

docs.title: Differential Expression
docs.text:
The differential expression workflow keeps HTML reports by default.

Pattern What it captures Why it is kept *.html Differential expression report Main user-facing analysis output.

docs.title: Files That Are Usually Excluded
docs.text:
The following file types are generally excluded unless a workflow explicitly adds them:

  • large intermediate BAM files
  • Nextflow work-directory internals
  • container cache files
  • temporary FASTQ files
  • unpublished tool scratch files
  • hidden system files

This is intentional. The archive is meant to contain final or inspection-ready outputs, not a complete copy of the computational workspace.

docs.title: User-Controlled Additions
docs.text:
Some UI options expand the archive by adding extra patterns:

Module UI option Added patterns Main consequence rnafusion Store alignments in binary format BAM *.Aligned.sortedByCoord.out.bam, *.Aligned.sortedByCoord.out.bam.bai, *.Chimeric.out.junction, *.SJ.out.tab Adds alignment and junction evidence; archive size can increase substantially. rnasplice Store alignments in binary format BAM *.sorted.bam, *.sorted.bam.bai Adds sorted alignment files; archive size can increase substantially. rnasplice Save R objects *.rds Adds R analysis objects for downstream inspection. rnavar Store alignments in binary format BAM *.aligned.bam, *.aligned.bam.bai Adds aligned variant-calling BAM files; archive size can increase substantially.

docs.title: Additional Work Directory Recovery
docs.text:
Most files are selected from the workflow resultsdir. However, some useful outputs may remain inside the Nextflow work directory if they are not published by the upstream pipeline.

Splyne supports a targeted recovery mechanism:

  1. Search the Nextflow work directory for a specific directory name.
  2. Copy selected file extensions into resultsdir/extra_splyne/.
  3. Preserve relative paths to avoid filename collisions.
  4. Run the normal archive filtering step.

Currently, this is used by rnafusion to recover PDF files from microH_expr_brkpt_plots.

docs.title: Recovery and Run Inspector
docs.text:
When a run is recovered through the Run Inspector, Splyne uses the ft_path stored in the run registry. This means recovered archives follow the same filtering rules that were selected when the workflow was launched.

If filetypes.txt is missing or the results/work directories no longer exist, recovery archiving may fail because the archiver no longer knows which files should be retained.

docs.title: Considerations
docs.text:
Filtering depends on upstream output names. If an nf-core pipeline changes its published file names or extensions, the corresponding allowed_ft patterns may need to be updated. This is quite unlikely to happen, since Splyne follows a fixed-release strategy for each workflow, although this possibility cannot be fully excluded.

The filtering system is inclusive: files are kept only if they match at least one allowed pattern. A valid result file with an unexpected extension will not be archived unless the pattern list is updated.

docs.title: Result Packaging
docs.text:
Splyne packages workflow outputs into ZIP archives after each workflow completes.

flowchart TD

    subgraph Configuration
    A["Workflow page"] --> B["Define allowed_ft patterns"]
    B --> C["Workflow is launched"]
    C --> D["Job manager writes filetypes.txt"]
    C --> E["Workflow completes"]
    end

    subgraph Archiving
    E --> F["Zip archiver reads filetypes.txt"]
    F --> G["Scan results"]
    G --> H["Keep matching files"]
    H --> I["Create ZIP with filtered results"]
    end

    subgraph Cleaning
    I --> J["Cleanup intermediate files"]
    end

docs.title: Storage Location
docs.text:
Archives are stored under:

temp_files/stored_results/

docs.title: Archive Naming
docs.text:
Archive names encode:

  • run ID with timestamp
  • pipeline name
  • execution status

Example:

run_27052026_203444_nf-core-rnavar_success.zip

docs.title: Status Labels
docs.text:
Possible status suffixes include:

  • success
  • cancelled
  • incomplete
  • finished-or-unknown

docs.title: Run History
docs.text:
The Run History page displays available ZIP files as cards with:

  • run identifier
  • pipeline name
  • date and time
  • status
  • archive size
  • download action
  • delete action

By default, the application keeps the most recent stored runs and removes older archives according to the configured retention policy, which is defined at 15 runs.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
After an archive is successfully created, temporary workflow directories are cleaned to reduce disk usage.

Cleanup includes the workflow work directory and output directory used for the completed run. For the differential expression workflow, the temporary uploaded data directory is also cleared after successful packaging.

docs.title: Relationship With Result Filtering
docs.text:
Run History only displays ZIP archives that were created after filtering. It is critical to understand that the files shown to the user are therefore not a complete mirror of the original Nextflow results directory.

The exact contents of each archive depend on:

  • the workflow-specific default patterns
  • optional UI choices that add extra patterns
  • whether additional work-directory recovery was enabled for the workflow
  • whether the upstream pipeline published files using expected names

See Results > Filtering Logic for the full pattern list and selection behavior.

docs.title: Design goal
docs.text:
Splyne is built with simplicity as a core principle, emphasizing a clean and constrained interface for pipeline execution.

The UI is structured around a persistent left-side sidebar and a single active main page. User interaction is limited to clearly defined and unambiguous controls, ensuring that available options remain interpretable without requiring prior expertise.

Pipeline modules are intentionally atomic and sequential, guiding users through a stepwise execution process. Advanced configuration and non-essential parameters are encapsulated within collapsible, informational sections and are not required for standard operation or successful workflow execution.

The interface prioritizes clarity and minimalism, exposing only essential functionality while retaining access to advanced settings for expert users when needed.

docs.title: Sidebar
docs.text:
The application provides a persistent sidebar that includes:

  • screen mode selector
  • process status indicator
  • action dashboard
  • version and github repository link

By default, it also includes the application navigation system, although this can be configured according to user preferences.

docs.title: Screen mode
docs.text:
The application provides three navigation display modes:

  • sidebar
  • top
  • hidden

The default mode is sidebar, where Splyne pages are presented in the left-hand sidebar. In top mode, pages are shown in a top navigation bar, whereas hidden mode removes the navigation menu from the interface.

The selected mode is stored in session state and can be changed when no long-running process is active.

docs.title: Process status indicator
docs.text:
To facilitate the management of long-running processes, the sidebar includes a visual indicator reflecting the current job state stored in session state.

If no process is active, the indicator remains disabled and no actions are available. When a process is running, the sidebar displays an active status badge along with a button to cancel the ongoing process. The process ID is displayed as a placeholder.

Inactive process marker Active process marker

docs.title: Action dashboard
docs.text:
The sidebar action dashboard includes controls for:

file_copy clearing fastp-filtered temporary reads

cached resetting the application state

power_settings_new shutting down the application

These actions are disabled while a long-running process is active to prevent orphan processes or inconsistent results caused by unexpected interactions.

docs.title: User feedback
docs.text:
The UI uses:

  • badges for workflow stage and status
  • toasts for transient process updates
  • warnings for invalid or missing prerequisites
  • popovers for help text and log views
  • interactive tables for samplesheets and metadata review

docs.title: Differential Expression
docs.text: This page documents Splyne's differential expression post-processing module.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The differential expression module runs a dedicated Nextflow workflow around an R/Quarto analysis script for count-based expression analysis. It is not a nf-core workflow but a custom-developed analytical script following conventional procedures, with DESeq2 R package for gene-level differential expression analysis and clusterProfiler for gene-set enrichment analysis.

The workflow has been specifically designed to leverage the raw gene-level count matrices generated by Salmon within the nf-core/rnasplice pipeline. Thereby, the expected user behaviour is:

  • Run a differential splicing analysis.
  • Retrieve the tximport/salmon.merged.gene_counts.tsv file from the pipeline results directory.
  • Prepare a dedicated metadata table in tab-separated values (tsv) format.
  • Execute the current module.

In any case, the workflow accepts any gene-level count matrix following the input structure described below. Therefore, users may also provide count matrices generated with alternative quantification or counting tools, provided that the matrix format remains compatible with the expected input specification.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A gene count table must be available.
  • A metadata table should be created accordingly.
  • Both tables must refer to the same samples to be compatible.
  • The selected dependency profile must support the R/Quarto workflow.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Users upload:

  • gene count table
  • metadata table

Accepted file extensions:

  • .tsv
  • .csv
  • .txt

Splyne stores normalized working copies under:

temp_files/nf-dea-temp/data/

docs.title: Metadata table
docs.text:
sample condition sample_1 treatment sample_2 control ... ... sample_n treatment

Warning

Be aware that encoding issues may arise when sample names contain complex or special characters. It is recommended to minimize the use of special characters as much as possible.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Advanced options expose common statistical thresholds:

  • CPM filtering threshold
  • minimum number of samples
  • adjusted significance threshold
  • log fold-change threshold

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: UI parameter Pipeline argument or internal variable Default Possible values Consequence Dependency profile -profile apptainer apptainer, docker Selects the dependency backend used by the differential expression Nextflow workflow. CPM threshold SPLYNE_CPM_THR environment variable 1.0 Decimal from 0.0 to 10.0, step 0.1 Minimum counts-per-million expression required for a gene to be retained. Higher values remove more low-expression genes. Minimum samples threshold SPLYNE_NSAMPLES_THR environment variable 2 Integer from 1 to 100 Minimum number of samples in which each gene must be expressed. Higher values make expression filtering more stringent. Error rate limit SPLYNE_ALPHA_THR environment variable 0.05 Decimal from 0.00 to 0.10, step 0.01 Statistical significance cutoff used by the analysis script. Lower values reduce false positives but may reduce sensitivity. Log2 fold-change threshold SPLYNE_LOGFC_THR environment variable 1.5 Decimal from 0.0 to 5.0, step 0.1 Minimum effect size required for a result to be considered biologically meaningful. Higher values focus on larger expression changes.

docs.title: Execution
docs.text:
Splyne builds the nextflow run differential_expression.nf command and submits it through the shared job manager as a declarative Workflow instance.

The process is monitored in the same way as the nf-core workflow pages. When the run completes, selected outputs are archived for Run History.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Outputs are generated by the dedicated Nextflow workflow and include:

  • Quality control and exploratory analysis
  • Expression filtering and normalization
  • Principal component analysis (PCA)
  • Differential gene expression analysis
  • DEA visualization through volcano plots and heatmaps
  • Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis
  • MSigDB Hallmark pathway enrichment analysis

See Results > Filtering logic for more information on ouput filtration.

docs.title: Notes and Limitations
docs.text: The module assumes that count and metadata tables have compatible sample definitions. It checks dimensions before execution, but users remain responsible for ensuring that sample names and experimental groups are biologically correct.

docs.title: Input and Samplesheets
docs.text: This page documents the input discovery and samplesheet generation stage.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The input module converts a user-selected directory of sequencing files into a samplesheet that can be consumed by downstream nf-core workflows.

By design, all nf-core pipelines require a standardized samplesheet in CSV format, which serves as the primary entry point for defining input data and associated sample metadata. This samplesheet typically consists of a set of required columns that describe each biological sample and link it to its corresponding sequencing files. At minimum, it includes a unique sample identifier and the file paths to the corresponding reads, with optional additional fields depending on the specific pipeline (such as strandedness, replicate information, or batch metadata).

A typical paired-end samplesheet looks simmilar to this, with each row represented as comma-separated values:

sample,fastq_1,fastq_2
S1,/path/to/S1_R1.fastq.gz,/path/to/S1_R2.fastq.gz
S2,/path/to/S2_R1.fastq.gz,/path/to/S2_R2.fastq.gz

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Input files must be available locally.
  • Files should be grouped in a single directory.
  • File names should follow Splyne's naming conventions.
  • Only one supported file format is allowed per run
  • Paired-end files should share the same base name
  • Data must be properly formatted and free of corruption

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Supported file types:

  • .fastq
  • .fq
  • .fastq.gz
  • .fq.gz
  • .bam
  • .cram

Mixed input classes are not supported in the same dataset.

docs.title: File naming conventions
docs.text:
The Splyne Upload reads module is designed to automatically process sequencing data based on defined file naming rules. Proper adherence to these conventions ensures correct sample detection, pairing, and downstream processing.

sampleName[_R1/R2].extension -> sampleName[_R1/R2].fastq | sampleName.bam/cram
  • sampleName: the name of the sample, must not contain underscores _
  • _R1 or _R2: read pair indicator for paired-end samples (will be ignored if single-end or aligned reads are provided)
  • .extension: allowed file extension (fastq, bam, cram)

Guidelines:

  • Do not use underscores inside sample names.
  • Use simple sample names when possible
  • Use _R1 and _R2 for paired-end reads.
  • Avoid special characters in file names (spaces, asterisks, etc.)
  • Use dashes for long sampleNames, e.g. sample1-treatment-VEGF-12h

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: The input stage has minimal configuration. Users select a directory and then review the samplesheet, which is visualized as an editable table with varying attributes (columns) depending on whether raw or aligned reads have been provided.

docs.title: Execution
docs.text:
Splyne scans the selected directory, classifies supported files and creates temp_files/samplesheet.csv.

If uncompressed FASTQ files are found, Splyne launches pigz as a managed process and stores the resulting .gz paths for downstream use.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
The input stage produces:

  • detected read file paths in session state
  • temp_files/samplesheet.csv
  • optionally compressed FASTQ files derived from uncompressed input

docs.title: Notes and Limitations
docs.text: Automatic parsing depends on file names. If samples are not detected correctly, users should simplify names or manually adjust the editable samplesheet before continuing.

docs.title: Read Preprocessing and Quality Control
docs.text: This page documents Splyne's quality-control-oriented workflows: direct read preprocessing with fastp and quality-control execution through nf-core/demo.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The preprocessing stage helps users inspect and clean raw RNA-seq reads before downstream analysis. It is optional because several nf-core workflows already include internal quality-control steps. Aligned BAM or CRAM inputs bypass read filtering and should proceed directly to analysis workflows.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Input files must be uploaded through the input module.
  • The samplesheet must be generated and saved.
  • fastp preprocessing requires paired-end FASTQ files.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
The module consumes the current saved samplesheet and the paths stored in session state after input detection.

Supported fastp inputs:

  • .fastq.gz
  • .fq.gz

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The fastp page exposes default parameters and an advanced editor for selected filtering settings, including:

  • failed read storage
  • N-base threshold
  • Phred score limit
  • minimum read length
  • average quality filtering
  • low-complexity filtering
  • personalized adapter trimming

docs.title: fastp Read Filtering
docs.text: UI parameter fastp argument or internal variable Default Possible values Consequence R1 output file name output path passed to -o clean_r1 Text without spaces Controls the suffix used for filtered R1 files. Splyne prefixes the selected sample name automatically. R2 output file name output path passed to -O clean_r2 Text without spaces Controls the suffix used for filtered R2 files. Splyne prefixes the selected sample name automatically. Store failed reads --failed_out false true, false Stores reads that fail filters in failed_reads.txt. Useful for debugging, but increases temporary storage. Maximum number of N bases per read -n 5 Integer from 0 to 15 Discards reads containing more unassigned bases than the selected threshold. Lower values are stricter. Phred score threshold -q 15 Integer from 10 to 30 Defines the base-quality threshold used to classify low-quality bases. Higher values are stricter. Allowed percentage of unqualified bases -u 40 Integer from 0 to 100 Discards reads when the percentage of bases below the Phred threshold exceeds this value. Lower values are stricter. Minimum average read quality -e 0 Integer from 0 to 40 Discards reads whose average quality is below this value. The default keeps this filter effectively permissive. Deactivate read length filter -L when enabled false true, false Disables length filtering. When disabled, -l is used with the selected minimum length. Minimum read length -l 15 Integer from 0 to 100 Discards reads shorter than the selected length. Ignored when read length filtering is deactivated. Activate low complexity filter -y false true, false Enables filtering of repetitive or low-complexity reads. Low complexity threshold -Y 30 Integer from 0 to 100 Defines the minimum sequence complexity required when low-complexity filtering is active. Higher values are stricter. Manual sequence trimming --adapter_fasta Empty FASTA-formatted text Provides custom adapter or sequence trimming targets. Invalid FASTA content may cause fastp execution errors. docs.title: Gene Fusion Detection
docs.text: This page documents the Splyne integration for nf-core/rnafusion. For details on workflow functionalities, visit the official documentation of the pipeline in nf-core website.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The module detects candidate gene fusion events from RNA-seq data using multiple fusion-calling tools.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Input files must be uploaded and validated.
  • The samplesheet must be saved.
  • Reference resources must be available.
  • A Nextflow dependency profile must be available, preferably Apptainer or Docker.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
The workflow uses one of the available samplesheets:

  • temp_files/samplesheet.csv for raw input files.
  • temp_files/clean_samplesheet.csv when fastp preprocessing has generated cleaned reads.

Splyne automatically selects the cleaned samplesheet when available, although the user may explicitly specify which file should be used. Using the cleaned samplesheet allows for greater flexibility in customizing input file trimming and can reduce computational time by disabling QC checks in each workflow. In contrast, using raw reads is particularly useful when the goal is to maximize reproducibility.

The full workflow is available only when FASTQ files are provided. Although BAM files can be used as input, this is not the preferred option. First, the fusioncatcher fusion detection tool only accepts FASTQ files, meaning that the use of aligned reads restricts the available fusion callers to arriba and star-fusion. Moreover, as described in the nf-core/rnafusion documentation, BAM compatibility and fusion detection is highly dependent on the parameters defined in the alignment command. To ensure the analytical success, provide FASTQ files when available.

docs.text:
Default execution uses:

  • nf-core/rnafusion

  • GRCh38/Gencode-46 reference setup
  • Apptainer execution profile

Advanced options expose selected pipeline parameters, including dependency profile, selected fusion tools, tool-support thresholds and optional output retention.

docs.title: Execution
docs.text:
Splyne builds the nextflow run nf-core/rnafusion command from the selected UI parameters and submits it through the shared job manager as a declarative Workflow instance.

During execution, the workflow page displays process status and a Nextflow log popover. When the process exits, Splyne launches the result archiver.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: Archived outputs include selected reports, summary tables, fusion-caller outputs and workflow metadata according to the module's filtering patterns. See Results > Filtering logic for more information on ouput filtration.

docs.title: Notes and Limitations
docs.text: Fusion detection can be resource-intensive and may generate large intermediate files. Retaining additional outputs should be enabled only when the user has sufficient storage and a clear downstream need.

docs.title: Differential Splicing
docs.text: This page documents the Splyne integration for nf-core/rnasplice. For details on workflow functionalities, visit the official documentation of the pipeline in nf-core website.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The module is focused on detecting differential splicing events between groups from RNA-seq data using a standardized nf-core workflow.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Input files must be uploaded and validated.
  • The samplesheet must be saved.
  • Reference resources must be available.
  • Experimental conditions must be correctly represented in the samplesheet.
  • A contrastsheet must define the comparison of interest.
  • A Nextflow dependency profile must be available, preferably Apptainer or Docker.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
The workflow uses one of the available samplesheets:

  • temp_files/samplesheet.csv for raw input files.
  • temp_files/clean_samplesheet.csv when fastp preprocessing has generated cleaned reads.

Splyne also uses a contrastsheet for treatment-control comparisons.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The module exposes selected workflow parameters through the advanced options panel. Users can review samplesheet and contrastsheet content before execution.

The default contrast follows a treatment-versus-control structure and should be reviewed against the experimental design. However, despite this naming convention, it can be used to compare any two-level groups. This structure is mainly adopted as a bioinformatics convention, but there is no limitation preventing other types of contrast, such as sex-based comparisons, time1 versus time2, etc.

docs.text:
Splyne builds the nextflow run nf-core/rnasplice command from the selected UI parameters and submits it through the shared job manager as a declarative Workflow object.

During execution, Splyne monitors the active process, displays the Nextflow log and prevents conflicting long-running jobs from being launched.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: Results are packaged after completion and made available from Run History. Output filtering focuses on interpretable reports, tables, plots and workflow summary artifacts. See Results > Filtering logic for more information on ouput filtration.

docs.title: Notes and Limitations
docs.text: Differential splicing results depend strongly on correct experimental metadata. Users should verify sample conditions and contrasts before launch.

docs.title: RNA Variant Calling
docs.text: This page documents the Splyne integration for nf-core/rnavar. For details on workflow functionalities, visit the official documentation of the pipeline in nf-core website.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The variant calling module detects and optionally annotates genetic variants that can be retrieved from RNA-seq data.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Input files must be uploaded and validated.
  • The samplesheet must be saved.
  • Reference resources must be available.
  • Read length parameter must be reviewed.
  • A Nextflow dependency profile must be available, preferably Apptainer or Docker.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
The workflow uses one of the available samplesheets:

  • temp_files/samplesheet.csv for raw input files.
  • temp_files/clean_samplesheet.csv when fastp preprocessing has generated cleaned reads.

docs.title: BAM input considerations
docs.text: If aligned reads are provided and base recalibration is intended to be activated, it is crucial to ensure that the corresponding alignment files contain compatible sequence dictionary headers. For instance, pipeline may fail if baserecalibration is enabled and no specified sequencing platform is available in BAM header.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Advanced options expose selected parameters for:

  • sequencing platform
  • STAR BAM sorting
  • duplicate removal
  • GATK filtering
  • base recalibration
  • variant annotation
  • optional BAM retention

Splyne also checks for optional resources:

  • variation databases for base recalibration
  • snpEff and VEP cache directories for variant annotation

If these resources are missing, Splyne disables the corresponding steps and informs the user.

docs.title: Execution
docs.text:
Splyne builds the nextflow run nf-core/rnavar command from the selected UI parameters and submits it through the shared job manager as a declarative Workflow object.

During execution, the page reports process state and exposes the Nextflow log. After completion, Splyne archives selected outputs into Run History.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: Archived files include selected HTML reports, VCF files, VCF indexes, annotation tables, CSV/TXT summaries and pipeline parameter files. If BAM retention is enabled, selected alignment files are added to the archive filters. See Results > Filtering logic for more information on ouput filtration.

docs.title: Notes and Limitations
docs.text: RNA variant calling has known biological and technical constraints, including expression bias, allele-specific expression and alignment artifacts. Results should be interpreted with appropriate downstream validation.
